title: Kubernetes for Machine Learning
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Kubernetes for Machine Learning ##### ₹6.8 lakh for GPUs nobody was using A company in Gurugram moved their ML services to a GPU-enabled Kubernetes cluster. Three months later, finance flagged a ₹6.8 lakh monthly bill for a workload that should have cost about ₹1.5 lakh. Two causes. First, their inference deployment had no resource `requests`, so Kubernetes scheduled pods anywhere and the cluster autoscaler kept adding GPU nodes it could not bin-pack. Second, their training jobs requested a full GPU each and ran for 20 minutes an hour — the nodes stayed up 24/7 because the autoscaler's scale-down was blocked by a DaemonSet with no pod-disruption tolerance. The fixes were configuration, not architecture: correct requests and limits, a taint on the GPU node pool so CPU pods stopped landing there, `scale-down-unneeded-time` tuned, and training moved to `Job` resources on a spot node pool. The bill dropped to ₹1.6 lakh. Kubernetes gives ML teams real capability — GPU scheduling, autoscaling, rolling deploys, self-healing. It also gives you many ways to spend money on nothing. Both come from the same set of primitives. ##### Core objects, in ML terms | Object | What it is | ML use | |---|---|---| | **Pod** | One or more containers sharing network and storage | A model server instance | | **Deployment** | Manages a ReplicaSet of identical pods | Stateless inference service | | **Service** | Stable virtual IP and DNS across pods | `http://embedder.ml.svc.cluster.local` | | **Ingress** | External HTTP routing and TLS | Public API endpoint | | **Job / CronJob** | Run-to-completion workloads | Training runs, batch scoring | | **StatefulSet** | Stable identity and storage per pod | Vector DB, distributed training ranks | | **ConfigMap / Secret** | Configuration and credentials | Model config, API keys | | **PVC** | Persistent storage claim | Model weights, checkpoints | | **HPA** | Scales pod count on metrics | Traffic-driven inference scaling | The mental model that makes Kubernetes click: you declare **desired state**, and a control loop continuously reconciles reality toward it. You never say "start three pods" — you say "three pods should exist", and the controller makes it so, forever, including after a node dies. ##### Deploying a model service ```yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: llm-inference namespace: ml spec: replicas: 2 selector: matchLabels: {app: llm-inference} template: metadata: labels: {app: llm-inference} annotations: prometheus.io/scrape: "true" prometheus.io/port: "8000" spec: nodeSelector: cloud.google.com/gke-accelerator: nvidia-l4 tolerations: - key: nvidia.com/gpu operator: Exists effect: NoSchedule # only GPU workloads land on GPU nodes terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120 # let in-flight generations finish initContainers: - name: fetch-model image: google/cloud-sdk:slim command: ["gsutil", "-m", "cp", "-r", "gs://models/mistral-7b-awq", "/models/"] volumeMounts: [{name: model-cache, mountPath: /models}] containers: - name: vllm image: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/proj/ml/vllm-server:1.14.2 # never :latest args: ["--model", "/models/mistral-7b-awq", "--quantization", "awq", "--gpu-memory-utilization", "0.90", "--max-model-len", "8192"] ports: [{containerPort: 8000, name: http}] resources: requests: cpu: "4" memory: 24Gi nvidia.com/gpu: 1 limits: cpu: "8" memory: 32Gi nvidia.com/gpu: 1 # GPU: requests MUST equal limits startupProbe: # model loading takes minutes httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000} failureThreshold: 60 periodSeconds: 10 readinessProbe: # remove from Service when overloaded httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000} periodSeconds: 5 livenessProbe: # restart only if genuinely wedged httpGet: {path: /health, port: 8000} periodSeconds: 20 failureThreshold: 6 volumeMounts: - {name: model-cache, mountPath: /models} - {name: shm, mountPath: /dev/shm} volumes: - {name: model-cache, emptyDir: {sizeLimit: 60Gi}} - {name: shm, emptyDir: {medium: Memory, sizeLimit: 8Gi}} # PyTorch needs this ``` Four ML-specific details in there that people learn the hard way: - **`startupProbe`** — a 7B model takes two to five minutes to load. Without a startup probe, the liveness probe kills the pod mid-load, forever. This is the single most common ML-on-Kubernetes failure. - **`/dev/shm`** — PyTorch DataLoader workers use shared memory, and Docker's 64 MB default causes cryptic `Bus error` crashes. - **`terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120`** — the default 30 seconds cuts off in-flight generations. Combine with a `preStop` hook and graceful shutdown in the app. - **Pinned image tags.** `:latest` in a Deployment means you cannot reproduce or roll back. ##### GPU scheduling GPUs are an *extended resource* exposed by the NVIDIA device plugin (a DaemonSet). They are **not overcommittable** — `requests` must equal `limits`, and a GPU is allocated whole to one container by default. That whole-GPU granularity is expensive when a small embedding model needs 4 GB of an 80 GB A100. Three sharing mechanisms: | Mechanism | Isolation | Use for | |---|---|---| | **Time-slicing** | None (shared memory, context switching) | Dev, notebooks, bursty small models | | **MPS** | Weak | Multiple small inference services | | **MIG** (A100/H100) | Hardware-partitioned, strong | Production multi-tenant | ```yaml # Time-slicing config for the NVIDIA device plugin sharing: timeSlicing: resources: - name: nvidia.com/gpu replicas: 4 # one physical GPU advertised as 4 schedulable units ``` Organise GPU capacity into **node pools** with distinct machine types, and **taint** them so only pods that tolerate the taint are scheduled there. Without the taint, ordinary CPU pods land on your ₹300/hour GPU nodes and block scale-down. For distributed training, use the Kubeflow Training Operator's `PyTorchJob`, which handles rank assignment, master addressing and gang scheduling: ```yaml apiVersion: kubeflow.org/v1 kind: PyTorchJob metadata: {name: finetune-7b} spec: runPolicy: {cleanPodPolicy: Running, backoffLimit: 2} pytorchReplicaSpecs: Master: replicas: 1 template: {spec: {containers: [{name: pytorch, image: ..., resources: {limits: {nvidia.com/gpu: 8}}}]}} Worker: replicas: 3 template: {spec: {containers: [{name: pytorch, image: ..., resources: {limits: {nvidia.com/gpu: 8}}}]}} ``` Gang scheduling matters: without it (via Volcano or Kueue), Kubernetes may schedule 3 of your 4 workers, and they will sit holding GPUs while waiting for a fourth that never arrives — a classic distributed-training deadlock. ##### Autoscaling ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Traffic rises] --> B[HPA reads custom metric:
queue depth or TTFT p95] B --> C{Above target?} C -->|Yes| D[Increase replica count] D --> E{Enough node capacity?} E -->|No| F[Cluster autoscaler adds a GPU node] F --> G[Node ready: 3-6 min for GPU + driver] G --> H[Pod pulls image and loads model: 2-5 min] H --> I[Readiness probe passes, traffic flows] C -->|No, and sustained low| J[Scale down after stabilization window] ``` **HPA** scales pod count. The formula is simple: `desired = ceil(current × currentMetric / targetMetric)`. CPU utilisation is a poor signal for GPU inference — the GPU saturates long before the CPU does. Scale on a **custom metric** instead: ```yaml apiVersion: autoscaling/v2 kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler metadata: {name: llm-inference} spec: scaleTargetRef: {apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: llm-inference} minReplicas: 2 maxReplicas: 12 metrics: - type: Pods pods: metric: {name: llm_queue_depth} target: {type: AverageValue, averageValue: "8"} behavior: scaleUp: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 30 policies: [{type: Pods, value: 4, periodSeconds: 60}] scaleDown: stabilizationWindowSeconds: 600 # long: model loading is expensive policies: [{type: Percent, value: 25, periodSeconds: 120}] ``` The asymmetric behaviour is deliberate: scale up fast because users are waiting, scale down slowly because a new pod costs 5–10 minutes of model loading and you do not want to thrash. **Cluster Autoscaler** (or Karpenter, which is faster and better at instance-type selection) adds and removes nodes. The end-to-end cold start for a GPU pod is genuinely slow — 3–6 minutes for the node plus 2–5 for model loading. Mitigate with a warm baseline (`minReplicas: 2`), **overprovisioning** via low-priority placeholder pods that get evicted when real work arrives, and node-local model caching so pods do not re-download 14 GB. **KEDA** extends HPA to scale on external signals — Kafka lag, SQS depth, a Prometheus query — including scale-to-zero for batch and dev workloads. ##### KServe KServe adds an ML-native abstraction on top: one `InferenceService` gives you autoscaling (including scale-to-zero), canary traffic splitting, a standard prediction protocol, and optional transformer and explainer components. ```yaml apiVersion: serving.kserve.io/v1beta1 kind: InferenceService metadata: {name: fraud-scorer, namespace: ml} spec: predictor: minReplicas: 1 maxReplicas: 10 scaleTarget: 20 scaleMetric: concurrency canaryTrafficPercent: 10 # 10% to the new revision model: modelFormat: {name: sklearn} storageUri: gs://models/fraud/v7 resources: requests: {cpu: "2", memory: 4Gi} limits: {cpu: "4", memory: 8Gi} transformer: containers: - name: feature-prep image: .../feature-prep:2.1.0 ``` `canaryTrafficPercent` in a single field is the reason teams adopt KServe — doing progressive rollout by hand with Deployments and Services is fiddly and error-prone. ##### Helm Raw YAML across dev, staging and production means three copies that drift. Helm templates them. ```yaml # values-prod.yaml replicaCount: 4 image: {repository: asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/proj/ml/vllm-server, tag: "1.14.2"} model: {uri: gs://models/mistral-7b-awq, maxLen: 8192, quantization: awq} resources: requests: {cpu: "4", memory: 24Gi, nvidia.com/gpu: 1} limits: {cpu: "8", memory: 32Gi, nvidia.com/gpu: 1} autoscaling: {enabled: true, minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 12, targetQueueDepth: 8} ``` ```bash helm upgrade --install llm ./charts/llm-service -f values-prod.yaml -n ml --atomic --timeout 15m helm rollback llm 0 -n ml # instant rollback to the previous release ``` `--atomic` rolls back automatically if the release fails to become ready — exactly what you want when a model fails to load at 2 AM. ##### Resource limits and cost control The requests-versus-limits distinction is where the money is: - **`requests`** — guaranteed, used for scheduling and bin-packing. Set too low and pods get evicted or throttled; set too high and you waste capacity. - **`limits`** — the hard cap. Exceeding memory limits means an immediate `OOMKilled`. Exceeding CPU limits means throttling, which shows up as mysterious latency. Recommendations for ML workloads: memory requests should equal limits (models have predictable footprints, and OOMKill is worse than waste); CPU requests should be realistic with generous limits (throttling an inference server's tokeniser hurts p99 badly); GPU requests must equal limits, always. Cost controls that compound: `ResourceQuota` and `LimitRange` per namespace; spot or preemptible node pools for training (60–90% cheaper, with checkpointing to survive preemption); scale-to-zero for dev and batch via KEDA; right-sizing from actual usage via VPA in recommendation mode; and cost attribution with Kubecost or OpenCost broken down by namespace and label. ##### Common mistakes - No `startupProbe`, so liveness kills the pod during model loading. - Default 64 MB `/dev/shm`, causing DataLoader crashes. - No taints on GPU node pools, letting CPU pods block scale-down. - Missing resource requests, so the scheduler cannot bin-pack. - Scaling GPU inference on CPU utilisation. - Symmetric scale-up/scale-down windows, causing thrash. - `:latest` image tags, making rollback impossible. - Distributed training without gang scheduling, deadlocking on partial placement. - Aggressive liveness probes restarting a pod that is merely busy. - No cost attribution, so nobody knows which team is spending what. ##### Hands-on Containerise a model service and deploy it with a Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, resource requests and limits, and all three probe types configured correctly for a slow-loading model. Add an HPA driven by a custom Prometheus metric, then generate load and watch it scale — record the time from load onset to a new pod serving traffic, and break that down into scheduling, image pull, and model load. For the mini-project, deploy an ML inference service on Kubernetes with GPU scheduling on a tainted node pool, KEDA or HPA autoscaling on queue depth, a parameterised Helm chart with dev and prod value files, a PodDisruptionBudget, and Prometheus scraping with a Grafana dashboard. Demonstrate scaling under load with a graph of replicas, latency and queue depth over time, and document your cold-start budget and how you mitigate it. Then write your HPA explanation — the scaling formula, why the metric choice matters for GPU workloads, and exactly what goes wrong when requests and limits are unset. ##### Key takeaways - Kubernetes reconciles declared desired state; probes are how it learns what "ready" means, and ML needs a startup probe. - GPUs are non-overcommittable extended resources — taint GPU pools, and use time-slicing or MIG for small models. - Scale on queue depth or latency, not CPU, and make scale-up fast while keeping scale-down slow. - Requests drive scheduling and cost; unset requests are how clusters silently become expensive. - Helm plus `--atomic`, spot pools for training, and per-namespace cost attribution are what keep the bill sane.
practical_task_reference: Containerize a model service and deploy it to a Kubernetes cluster with a deployment, service, resource limits, and horizontal pod autoscaling.
mini_project_reference: Deploy an ML inference service on Kubernetes with GPU scheduling, autoscaling, and a Helm chart, demonstrating scaling under load.
assignment_reference: Explain how horizontal pod autoscaling works and why setting resource requests/limits matters for ML workloads.
